title: The whole tractate
hook: sixty-four pages read; the siyum closes with a special Kaddish
tomorrow: you finished a tractate. so what's on the table?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shape of Berakhot: it opens with from when, and closes with peace. From time to peace. Now the whole thing is read. Is it done?

Graduation is called commencement, a word for beginning, said on the day something ends. Berakhot runs from page two to page sixty-four. Page two, because the Talmud's pages start there; some say it's a reminder that nobody ever truly starts at the beginning. And when the last page is done, the siyum closes with a Kaddish you don't hear on an ordinary day. So: finished, or begun? Inside the tradition, both answers have a voice.
screen: `COMMENCEMENT MEANS BEGINNING.` → `PAGE TWO TO SIXTY-FOUR.` → `FINISHED, OR BEGUN?`

segments.voice: First voice: it's finished, and that matters. A siyum, a completion, is a real occasion. People stop, read the last lines aloud, say the hadran, and celebrate. A whole tractate, learned from its first question to its last word, is something you can hold. It deserves a moment that says: you did this. Second voice: it's never finished. Rabbi Tarfon says in Pirkei Avot: it isn't on you to complete the work, and you aren't free to quit it. There's a custom, at a siyum, of reading the first lines of the next tractate before the celebration ends, so the learning never actually closes. Now listen to the Kaddish they say. This special Kaddish of the siyum speaks of a world that will be made new, and of God giving life to the dead. Something to tell a friend tonight: a form of that same Kaddish is also said at a burial. The words for the end of a book are the words for the end of a life, and both talk about renewal. So both voices win. The finish is real, and it's celebrated. The finish is also a door, and the custom walks right through it. A whole tractate isn't a trophy on a shelf. It's a ground to stand on for the next one. Finished, and begun.
screen: `FINISHED: A REAL OCCASION.` · `BEGUN: NOT YOURS TO COMPLETE.` · `THE FIRST LINES OF THE NEXT.` · `A KADDISH OF A WORLD MADE NEW.` · then, large: `FINISHED AND BEGUN.`

segments.voice: When a Kaddish is said, the people listening answer it. Say the answer once, slowly, out loud: amen, yehei shmei rabba mevarakh, may His great name be blessed forever. Then sit for a moment with the word amen, the yes that answers a prayer.
screen: `AMEN.` · `YEHEI SHMEI RABBA.` · `MAY HIS GREAT NAME BE BLESSED.`

segments.voice: The whole tractate. Berakhot, read from its first page to its last, and the custom of beginning again at once.
The line to keep: finished and begun, at the same time, in the same breath. Forty-nine of fifty.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3): debate shape. The two voices are 'it's finished' (the siyum as a real occasion) and 'it's begun' (Tarfon, Avot 2:16; the custom of reading the next tractate's opening). Both are voiced fairly; the script resolves with the carry, finished and begun.

'page two to page sixty-four': the tractate's folios run 2a–64a. 'Some say it's a reminder that nobody truly starts at the beginning' is a known homily (often attributed to Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev); voiced as 'some say'. Confirm.

The siyum Kaddish (Kaddish d'Itchadata / Kaddish d'Rabbanan practices differ): the long form mentioning the renewal of the world and reviving the dead is said at a siyum and at a burial in many rites. Confirm and soften if customs differ.
The custom of reading the opening of the next tractate (or the Hadran's link to the next) varies; voiced as 'there's a custom'. Confirm.
Practice: 'amen, yehei shmei rabba mevarakh' is the congregation's existing response, not a new prayer; the voice gives a short English gloss ('may His great name be blessed forever'). Confirm.
Noa storyline: Saba's group debates a break versus starting the next tractate right away; the siyum is tomorrow at Saba's apartment.
